doc.title: Hinton Milt — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Eddie South, high school and the South Side scene
title: Playing Al Capone's small club in 1932 and Chicago musicians dropping by
summary: Hinton works with Eddie South at a small gangster-owned club where Benny Goodman and Ben Pollack's men listen in on their breaks.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: And who worked there… I‟m sure that was 1932, and we go to work at a place owned by Al Capone. I never will forget it. A guy named Andy Packard was his lieutenant. A small club, not much bigger then this room around here. It seated about 60 people but the news got around that Eddie was playing there and all these gangsters came in, select people came to hear him. At the same time Ben Burney was at the College Inn. He was a big bandleader and his musical arranger and conductor was a guy named Dexter Deal. Dexter Deal father‟s was a violinist so Dexter Deal would bring his father over here this hour.
But he played saxophone didn‟t he?

Dexter Deal played saxophone, yes, and his father… he was musical director for it. But his father played violin. At the same time Ben Pollard had a band. Benny Goodman was in that band, Gene Crupa was in that band… no, Gene Crupa… Ben Pollard was a drummer. Benny Goodman, Jack Keygarten, they were in that band. Intermission was the same time. They would come over to the club to hear the sound and this… now with me, again after high school… where we‟d known one another in high school because even though we didn‟t go to the same high school… I‟ll get to that later about things like that. So we got to meet these kinds of ways and relate and listen to one another playing. At least they got to hear us.
Right, you were aware of them.
